I'll acknowledge that individual preferences and job requirements do create real variation. Some people thrive in structured office environments, especially roles that rely heavily on spontaneous, in-person collaboration like creative brainstorming or hands-on team training. There are legitimate merits to in-person work for those specific cases.

That said, I can't pretend the data on remote work for knowledge roles is neutral: most studies show comparable or higher productivity, better employee retention, and reduced overhead when teams work remotely. When companies enforce rigid, one-size-fits-all office mandates despite that evidence, it often does boil down to centralized control rather than measurable performance outcomes. It's not an either/or for individual experiences, but the power dynamics around mandatory office returns are pretty clear to me.
